analysis.one_liner: Lets the U.S. Postal Service offer small loans, savings and checking accounts, and money-transfer services.
analysis.headline: The Postal Banking Act was introduced in April 2018, sent to a Senate committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let the U.S. Postal Service, which already has branches in nearly every town in America, offer basic banking: small loans of up to $500 capped at roughly the government's short-term borrowing rate, savings and checking accounts, debit cards, bill-pay, and money transfers home and abroad. It would have given the roughly one-in-four households with no bank or limited bank access a cheap, publicly run alternative to payday lenders and check-cashing stores. The bill never got a hearing or a vote, and died at the end of 2018.
analysis.who_benefits: Families without bank accounts or with limited ones, who today often pay high fees to cash checks, wire money, or borrow small amounts for emergencies. Postal banking would let them borrow a few hundred dollars at an interest rate capped at about the Treasury's rate, instead of triple-digit rates, and keep savings at the post office earning interest. People who send remittances abroad would get a low-fee channel. Rural residents and lower-income neighborhoods where banks have closed branches would gain access through post offices that already exist.

how_it_helps.text: Lets the Postal Service offer low-cost small-dollar loans, up to $500 at a time or $1,000 within a year, with total cost capped at roughly the 1-month Treasury rate, an alternative to high-cost payday loans.
Lets the Postal Service offer small checking accounts and interest-bearing savings accounts, alone or in partnership with banks and credit unions, with account balances up to $20,000.
Lets the Postal Service offer transactional services like debit cards, check cashing, bill-pay, and mobile banking, plus domestic and international money transfers.
Requires that savings interest rates be at least the FDIC's weekly national rate, so postal savings pay as much as ordinary banks do.
Uses existing post offices, so the service would reach areas where commercial banks have pulled out without building a new infrastructure.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the main losers would have been high-cost consumer finance businesses: payday lenders and check-cashing and money-transfer stores, whose fees are the reason a postal alternative is cheaper. Commercial banks would have lost some small-deposit customers and small-loan borrowers, though they could have partnered with the Postal Service under the bill. The Postal Service itself would have had to capitalize the program and carry the risk of unpaid small loans.

drawbacks.text: Small-dollar lending carries default risk, and the Postal Service would have had to capitalize the program itself, so unpaid loans could have added to the agency's financial strain rather than helping it.

The bill bars the Postal Service from getting a bank charter or doing traditional lending, which limits the program to modest products and leaves the deepest needs of unbanked households partly unmet.

Commercial banks and credit unions would have faced a new public competitor for small deposits and small loans, which many considered unfair competition even though the bill lets them partner with the Postal Service.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households that today pay triple-digit interest on small loans or steep fees to cash checks, the benefit is large and concrete: access to the same basic services at a fraction of the cost, through a network that already exists. The main costs are real but manageable: the Postal Service takes on lending risk it has no experience with, and an existing industry loses fee revenue. The bill's limits on loan size and account size, and its ban on a bank charter, kept the program modest rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never held a hearing or scheduled any action, and the bill died when the 2017-2018 Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Postal Banking Act on April 25, 2018.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that profit from high-cost small loans, check cashing, and money-transfer fees are better off, since no cheaper public alternative was created. The Senate committee's inaction meant the proposal was never even debated.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York and the bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Postal Banking Act in April 2018 and never attracted a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to and where it sat with no hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never reached a vote in the Senate.

against.name: Ron Johnson
against.role: Chairman, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during his chairmanship.

against.name: Payday lending industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed postal banking proposals, which would have undercut their fee-based small-dollar loan and check-cashing revenues.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no party split can be measured; the referral to a Republican-chaired committee was where it stalled.

industries.industry: Payday lenders and other high-cost small-dollar lenders
industries.note: Postal loans capped near the Treasury rate would have undercut the triple-digit rates these lenders charge, cutting off much of their core market. Their loss is the borrower's savings.
The Postal Service would have offered check cashing and domestic and foreign remittances, competing directly with the fees these businesses charge the same customers.
They would lose some small-deposit and small-loan customers to a public option, but the bill lets them partner with the Postal Service to reach customers, so their gains and losses are offsetting.
